title: Kleene's Regular Expressions, Decades Before grep and sed
explainer: The pattern syntax inside grep, sed, awk, and shell globbing traces back to mathematician Stephen Kleene, who in the early 1950s described 'regular events' to characterize the behavior of simple neuron-inspired automata, work later published in 1956. Kleene's operators for union, concatenation, and repetition (the 'Kleene star') are exactly the operator set every regex engine still implements today. Ken Thompson carried the idea into Unix text tools in the late 1960s, which is why a formalism from automata theory now sits inside everyday shell scripts.

title: The Bourne Shell, and Why Bash Is Named for It
explainer: The scripting constructs that advanced shell work relies on - if/then, loops, functions, here-documents - were largely established by Stephen Bourne's shell, written at Bell Labs around 1977 as a successor to the original Unix shell. A decade later, Brian Fox wrote a free reimplementation for the GNU Project, released in 1989 and named 'bash' - the Bourne-Again Shell - as a direct homage. That lineage is why bash scripts still read like Bourne shell scripts with extensions added, rather than a clean break from them.
